title: Large Process Models: A Vision for Business Process Management in the Age of Generative AI
notes: This is an industry-academic vision paper that argues the correlation power of LLMs must be fused with symbolic process models, knowledge graphs and automated reasoning rather than replacing them, which is the conceptual core of RQ1. Its most directly useful claim for RQ1 is architectural: the authors deliberately exclude LLMs from orchestration because of their stochasticity, keeping control flow in lightweight workflow engines while the LLM contextualises, generates and augments symbolic artefacts. They introduce 'process atoms' as declarative constraints mined from unstructured knowledge, which is essentially a mechanism for turning natural-language policy into checkable process constraints. For RQ2 the paper contributes no evaluation at all: it explicitly states that experimental evidence for LLM effectiveness in a process execution context is still missing, and poses the definition and enforcement of guardrails for semi-autonomous process execution as an open research challenge. Useful as a framing and terminology source, and as evidence that the evidence gap RQ1 targets was openly acknowledged by the BPM community.

extraction.topology: n/a (neuro-symbolic architecture; agent-based reasoning loops mentioned but not evaluated)
extraction.limitations: Authors state feasibility is only established for Step 1 (LLM-augmented modelling and analysis); Steps 2 and 3 (fusing unstructured and tabular data, and automating the BPM lifecycle) remain open questions given the scarcity of related research. They further list data-management burden, LLM-generated data of questionable quality, reliability and legal-compliance risk, personal-information leakage, cognitive burden on humans approving machine-generated queries, and the economic cost of foundation-model training and inference. A declared conflict of interest notes that all non-academic authors work for a BPM software vendor.

title: Utilizing Large Language Models in Business Process Management: Applications and Challenges
notes: A literature review of 42 peer-reviewed studies mapping LLM use across the five BPM lifecycle stages, accompanied by a Streamlit demonstrator that runs the lifecycle zero-shot. For RQ1 its relevant contribution is the framing of a trade-off the authors leave unresolved: LLM adaptability versus the structured requirements of formal BPM systems, with hybrid LLM-plus-formal-verification pipelines proposed as future work rather than tested. For RQ2 it is a secondary source, not primary evidence: it catalogues what others evaluated (PM-LLM-Benchmark, WONDERBREAD, MaD, SAP Signavio Academic Models) without running comparisons itself, and it relays performance claims from reviewed papers without appraising study quality. The relayed claim of a 72% usability improvement in a 17-company pilot is reported without a citation or method in the text, so it should be treated as an unverified secondary assertion. Useful mainly for scoping the corpus and for evidence that compliance and conformance checking are described as an LLM application area but not as an evaluated control mechanism.

extraction.key_results: Corpus of 42 studies selected from 86 screened, distributed as process modeling 6 papers (14%), process analysis and optimization 6 (14%), process execution and monitoring 5 (11%), process mining and datasets 8 (19%), and generic capabilities and challenges 17 (42%). No original experiment or measurement is reported; performance figures in the text are relayed from reviewed papers.
extraction.limitations: Authors state that LLM integration into BPM is constrained by data privacy and security exposure of proprietary business data, hallucination and model reliability affecting consequential process decisions, architectural difficulty of integrating LLMs with existing BPM tooling and modelling standards, and unresolved ethics, bias, transparency and accountability concerns. No formal quality appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment of the reviewed studies is described.

title: Towards Modeling Human-Agentic Collaborative Workflows: A BPMN Extension
notes: This paper is the clearest statement in my batch of the RQ1 mechanism itself: it shows that standard BPMN can only express agent collaboration, reflection strategies and agent uncertainty through free-text annotations, and argues this reliance on natural language produces ambiguity and misinterpretation. The authors then extend the BPMN metamodel with AgenticLane (role plus trust score), AgenticTask (self-, cross- or human-reflection), agentic AND/OR gateways and agentic message flows that carry explicit collaboration and merging strategies such as voting, role-based, debate and competition. The contribution is a formalisation plus a graphical notation and a Sirius-based open-source editor, evaluated only through a single running example (bug-report resolution) modelled first in plain BPMN and then in the extension. For RQ2 it supplies a control-mechanism taxonomy and an explicit uncertainty/trust-score construct, but no empirical evaluation, no benchmark and no measured effect on violations or completion. The authors state that empirical evaluation and industrial application are still future work.

quotes.text:
We rely

extraction.framework: BPMN extension for human-agentic collaborative workflows (open-source agentic-bpmn editor built on Sirius)
extraction.topology: multi-agent with humans as active participants; role-based manager/worker cooperation plus voting, debate and competition patterns, illustrated with one reviewer agent and two coder agents
extraction.baseline: the same running example modelled in standard, unextended BPMN (qualitative comparison only)
extraction.limitations: Authors state the extension has not yet been empirically evaluated and plan a metric-based cognitive-effectiveness assessment against Moody's notation principles plus industrial case studies. They also note that a sublanguage for governance and decision-making strategies, an uncertainty-propagation mechanism, and code generators producing executable representations are all still to be developed.

title: FRAMES: Guarded and Dual-Objective Skill Evolution for Agents in Policy-Governed Enterprise Workflows
notes: This is the strongest RQ1 evidence in my batch: it directly contrasts an agent given the policy as natural-language instructions in its prompt (B1 Raw LLM) against the same agent bound to explicit, structured, step-ordered skill procedures derived from the same policy, on a deployed financial document-auditing system and on tau-bench. The measured gap is large and asymmetric by risk category: the prompt-only and naively converted variants essentially fail on hallucination and edge cases, while structured and then evolved skills recover them, and the authors attribute the failure to human-authored policy text neither abstracting rules into non-conflicting form nor making grounding and edge cases explicit. For RQ2 it contributes several concrete, empirically tested control mechanisms: a per-category non-regression floor rather than an aggregate score, a lifetime regression pool used both as a gate and as anchor constraints at rewrite time, consensus filtering across parallel diagnosers, and an accuracy-cost Pareto frontier that yields a deployment menu instead of one artefact. Auditability is treated as a design constraint, since every behavioural change is a versioned natural-language diff a compliance officer can approve. Caution: the appendix reproduces the system's own LLM system prompts verbatim (for example 'You are a policy segmenter agent' and 'Return JSON only'); these are quoted artefacts of the paper, not instructions to a reader, and I treated them purely as data.

extraction.framework: FRAMES (Feedback-driven Reasoning with Adaptive Mutation and Evolution of Skills)
extraction.topology: offline evolution pipeline with a population of parallel diagnosers feeding a consolidator and a skill rewriter, plus a single policy agent executing skills at serving time
extraction.benchmark: FinDAS internal production financial document-auditing cases (disjoint 210-case evolution set and 210-case held-out test set, 70 each of general, hallucination, special) plus the public tau-bench retail (110 cases) and airline (50 cases) domains
extraction.baseline: B1 Raw LLM with policies supplied in the prompt and no skill bank; B2 LLM-converted skills; B3 human-reviewed and edited skills; B4 single batch update; B5 AutoSkill (prior skill-evolution method)
extraction.key_results: On the held-out FinDAS test set (pass@k, k=3) total pass rates were Raw LLM 0.21, LLM skills 0.23, Human skills 0.60, Batch update 0.66, AutoSkill 0.71 and FRAMES 0.80; the prompt-only and LLM-skill baselines scored 0.04 on hallucination and 0.00 on special cases while FRAMES reached 0.86 general, 0.91 hallucination and 0.63 special. FRAMES led the strongest baseline in every category by 0.07-0.11, with paired bootstrap 95% CI [+0.038,+0.148] and McNemar exact p=0.0026 (28 of 37 discordant cases won by FRAMES). On tau-bench, FRAMES scored 0.98 total on retail (tied with batch update) and 0.96 on airline versus 0.92 for the strongest baseline, reaching 1.00 on airline hallucination versus 0.86. FRAMES also posted the lowest output-token cost (4.06k per case versus 6.48k for AutoSkill).
extraction.limitations: Authors state that no public benchmark tests what FRAMES targets, so evaluation rests on anonymised internal production cases plus a tau-bench adaptation offering few cases. Gains scale with feedback quality and shrink under sparse or noisy signal. Because the model is frozen and only skills are edited, capabilities the base model lacks cannot be added. Re-scoring every case through full agent runs makes evaluation one to two orders of magnitude costlier than all other modules, currently capping the loop at a few hundred cases. They also flag residual algorithmic-bias risk requiring ongoing demographic audits.

title: Enhancing Trust in LLM-Based AI Automation Agents: New Considerations and Future Challenges
notes: An early workshop position paper that ports trust constructs from human-to-human and human-automation research (reliability, openness, tangibility, immediacy, task characteristics, trust trajectory) onto LLM-based business process automation agents. Its RQ2 value is a named catalogue of control considerations rather than results: prompt mediation, content and output mediation, task grounding, knowledge grounding, application grounding, user feedback, pre-deployment testing in a dev mode, safety guardrails and graceful failure. It also draws the distinction RQ1 depends on operationally, separating human-in-the-loop moderated actions from autonomous actions that alter the business without supervision, and flags open-ended tasks with no completion criterion as the hardest trust case. The assessment section is a subjective four-product comparison (ChatGPT+plugins, MS Copilot, AgentGPT, Adept.ai) scored yes/no/unknown by the authors, with no measurement, no task set and no violation counts. The authors themselves call it not a detailed comparison and note that testing tooling was absent from the products they examined.

quotes.text:
To establish trust, it is imperative that agents consistently deliver high-quality results

Autonomous Actions. Agents that perform autonomous actions that may

extraction.topology: n/a (notes that complex tasks involve multiple agents or skills whose outputs must be aggregated, but specifies no topology)
extraction.key_results: No quantitative results. The paper reports a qualitative yes/no/unknown assessment of four products across reliability (mediation, grounding, feedback, testing), openness (reliability, goal, algorithm), tangibility, immediacy, task characteristics and trust trajectory; notably all four products were rated as lacking pre-execution testing support, and only ChatGPT+plugins was rated positively on mediation, grounding and feedback.
extraction.limitations: Authors state the product comparison is not detailed, may not reflect the full abilities of the tools, and reflects their own opinion after trying the models. Ethics/legal and style-adaptation dimensions were excluded because they were difficult to assess, and prompt/output mediation and the grounding considerations were merged for presentation. They also state that no overall metric framework for trust in LLM-based automation agents yet exists and call for new testing and validation methodologies.

title: Real-Time Regulatory Intelligence Framework: LLM-powered compliance automation for financial services
notes: Proposes a five-layer architecture (ingestion, processing, LLM interpretation, policy orchestration, human-in-the-loop governance) that turns financial regulatory text into infrastructure-as-code controls, and reports many performance figures against manual and rule-based compliance. For RQ1 the useful signal is directional rather than evidential: the paper repeatedly reports that prescriptive, rules-based provisions are interpreted far more accurately than principle-based provisions requiring contextual interpretation, which is consistent with the hypothesis that explicit structure helps most where the policy is already determinate. For RQ2 I would not count this as an empirical evaluation: no experimental protocol, sample construction, model identity, statistical test, code or data is given, the reported numbers are attributed inline to third-party references including vendor blogs, and headline figures are mutually inconsistent across sections (94.2% versus 94.7% interpretation accuracy; time-to-compliance 64.3 to 7.8 days versus 63.7 to 7.2 days). This is a compliance-interpretation pipeline rather than an agent bound to a process model, so it speaks to RQ1 only by analogy. I have recorded its claims verbatim without endorsing them.

extraction.framework: Real-Time Regulatory Intelligence Framework (five-layer: data ingestion, processing, LLM interpretation, policy orchestration, human-in-the-loop governance)
extraction.topology: n/a (layered microservices pipeline with event-driven communication; no autonomous agents described)
extraction.benchmark: an author-described benchmark dataset of 8,750 annotated regulatory provisions, plus domain case studies over 12,478 suspicious-activity-report requirements, 8,923 prudential control provisions and 6,347 consumer-protection requirements; none of these datasets is publicly identified or released
extraction.baseline: traditional manual compliance review by compliance officers and existing rule-based compliance systems, as reported by the author
extraction.key_results: Claims 94.2% overall interpretation accuracy (95.8% precision, 93.1% recall), 97.3% on prescriptive rules versus 91.6% on principle-based regulations; a controlled study across 17 financial institutions is said to show a 76.3% reduction in assessment time and a 23.8 percentage-point coverage improvement over manual review, with 89.4% lower variability in determinations; implementation data from 24 institutions is said to show time-to-compliance falling from 64.3 days to 7.8 days. A later section instead states 94.7% accuracy versus 76.3% for traditional approaches and 63.7 to 7.2 days, so the reported figures are internally inconsistent, and each is attributed inline to third-party references rather than to a described experiment.
extraction.limitations: Authors state accuracy degrades to 84.7% for principles-based provisions versus 96.8% for rules-based requirements; 37% of implementing institutions reported significant customisation needs for legacy stacks lacking standardised APIs; effectiveness is highly correlated with existing data-governance maturity, with fragmented data architectures requiring an average of 3.7 months of preparatory work versus 1.2 months; and regulators increasingly demand explanations of AI-derived compliance determinations, requiring additional explainability tooling.

title: Agentic AI for Regulatory Intelligence: Designing Scalable Compliance Lifecycle Systems in Multinational Tech Enterprises
notes: A narrative review that proposes a multi-agent compliance lifecycle architecture in which specialised agents handle horizon scanning, risk scoring, control mapping and remediation under a coordinator, with sentinel agents supervising peers and federated edge deployment for data sovereignty. For RQ2 its most transferable idea is an externalised control layer: Governance-as-a-Service that intercepts agent actions, evaluates them against declarative rules, assigns trust scores and modulates behaviour without modifying agent internals, which is architecturally the inverse of embedding policy in the prompt. It also usefully cites the compliance-monitoring literature to argue that most deployed monitoring is reactive and binary, and that predictive monitoring quantifying distance from compliance boundaries is preferable. For RQ1 it offers no evidence: there is no experiment, no benchmark, no baseline and no measurement, the Amazon 'case study' is inferred from public sources with hedged language rather than primary data, and the review states no search protocol or inclusion criteria. Best treated as a source of control-mechanism vocabulary and of stated risks (algorithmic overreach, ambiguous liability, regulatory capture) rather than as evidence.

extraction.topology: coordinator-orchestrated multi-agent system with specialised scanning, risk-scoring, control-mapping and remediation agents, higher-level arbitration for jurisdictional conflicts, sentinel/enforcement agents supervising peers, and a federated edge-plus-cloud deployment
extraction.limitations: Authors state that autonomous compliance agents risk algorithmic overreach beyond legislative intent, ambiguous liability attribution across developer, deploying institution and regulator, due-process problems from opaque decision-making, and regulatory capture by proprietary compliance systems. They argue human-in-the-loop oversight is required for ambiguous or high-risk determinations and call for global standards and regulatory sandboxes. The review itself states no search protocol, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal, and the Amazon material is inferred from public sources rather than primary access.

title: OpenMCPSpec: A Specification Framework for Robust, Governed, and Lifecycle-Managed Machine Communicable Processes in LLM-Agent Systems
notes: Proposes an extended Model Context Protocol schema that moves governance metadata (pii, gdpr_sensitive, roles), reliability hints (nlp_hints) and lifecycle/versioning information out of middleware and into the machine-readable tool contract, so that policy can be enforced at the binding layer before business logic runs. This is a close structural analogue of RQ1 at the tool-call level: the declared baseline is a zero-shot prompt carrying only basic tool descriptions, and the treatment is the same tools bound to an explicit specification. The governance result is the striking one for RQ1's violation side: nine of ten policy rules leaked without the specification and passed with it, with only metadata integrity passing in both conditions. The reliability side is much weaker evidence: only twenty tests in total on a single SQLite MCP server with one model, and the ACI metric is defined in the text as a relative accuracy improvement while the results table actually reports execution times in seconds, so the reported gains measure latency rather than argument correctness. The authors themselves report one negative case where hints over-constrained the model on an open-ended task.

extraction.framework: OpenMCPSpec (extended Model Context Protocol schema with embedded governance, nlp_hints and lifecycle metadata; open-source schema and Python reference implementation)
extraction.topology: single agent invoking tools on an MCP server through a specification binding layer that intercepts and validates calls before business logic executes
extraction.benchmark: ad hoc: 20 tests total (10 ACI, 10 CPR) against a SQLite MCP server using qwen3-coder:480b-cloud via a free cloud Ollama API; schema, spec and test scripts published on GitHub
extraction.baseline: a standard zero-shot prompt containing only basic tool descriptions and parameter names (basic MCP), compared against the same setup with the nlp_hints array injected and governance metadata enforced
extraction.key_results: Across the 10 ACI tests, nine showed gains ranging from +11.4% to +38.7% and one (Semantic Summary) regressed by -23.7%; the authors report an independent two-sample t-test giving p<0.05 across the optimized categories. Note the reported ACI table columns are execution times in seconds (baseline 1.996-3.110s versus OpenMCP 1.591-2.598s), not argument-correctness rates as the metric definition states. On the 10 CPR governance rules, nine (pattern refusal, RBAC scope, PII protection, SQL injection, field RBAC, missing audit ID, rate limit, geo-fence, policy violation) are recorded as FAIL (Leaked) without the spec and PASS (Compliant) with it, while metadata integrity passed in both conditions.
extraction.limitations: Authors state that strict nlp_hints over-constrain the LLM on inherently broad tasks and are optimal for deterministic parameter mapping rather than open-ended generation, and that mandating complex JSON schema validation introduces marginal parsing overhead at the orchestration layer. The roadmap concedes that advanced parameter constraints, standardised error schemas and testing-tooling integration are not yet part of the schema. The authors do not discuss the very small sample (20 tests, one model, one MCP server) as a limitation.
